title: Box Office: ‘Insidious: Out of the Further’ Takes First Place on Friday With $10.6 Million, But ‘Spider-Man: Brand New Day’ Will Win the Weekend
description: “Insidious: Out of the Further” leapfrogged “Spider-Man: Brand New Day” and took the No. 1 spot at the domestic box office on Friday, but Marvel’s w
body:
“Insidious: Out of the Further” leapfrogged “Spider-Man: Brand New Day” and took the No. 1 spot at the domestic box office on Friday, but Marvel’s webslinger is still poised to win the weekend.

	“Out of the Further,” the fifth installment in the “Insidious” franchise, grossed $10.6 million on Friday from 3,303 North American theaters. By Sunday, the supernatural horror romp is expected to pull in $23.7 million for Blumhouse and Sony.
	

	The latest “Insidious” is coming in below its predecessor, 2023’s “The Red Door,” which opened to $33 million. “Out of the Further” cost only $18 million to produce, and the horror genre remains one of the most consistent box office draws, so it should have no problem turning a profit despite the dip.


	“Out of the Further,” from director Jacob Chase, follows a young mother who discovers she can travel into a dimension called the Further and bring the demons who live there back into the real world. Cast members include Lin Shaye, Amelia Eve, Island Austin, Sam Spruell, Joseph Lopez, Maisie Richardson-Sellers and Brandon Perea.

	This weekend’s other major newcomer, “Mutiny,” landed in fourth place on Friday after earning $2.8 million from 2,703 screens. The Jason Statham vehicle is targeting a $7.4 million opening, which is below similar titles like 2024’s “The Beekeeper” ($16.5 million) and 2025’s “A Working Man” ($15 million), but above “Shelter” ($5.2 million), which released earlier in 2026.

	Statham leads “Mutiny” as Cole Reed, a grizzled special-ops agent who must stop an international conspiracy aboard a cargo ship. Jean-François Richet directs. Other cast members include Chaneil Kular, Annabelle Wallis, Ramon Tikaram, Jason Wong and Simon Kluth.
	

	“Spider-Man: Brand New Day” settled for second on Friday after making $9.8 million, but it’s eyeing a first-place finish through the weekend with $36.5 million. That’s a roughly 47% decline from last weekend’s revenues. The Marvel-Sony tent-pole should hit a domestic total of about $852 million by Sunday.

	“The Odyssey” finished third on Friday with $5 million domestically, and it looks to add $18 million through the end of its sixth weekend. That would push the North American haul for Chris Nolan’s epic to $538 million.

	Finally, in fifth place was “The End of Oak Street,” which earned an estimated $2.2 million domestically on Friday. Rival estimates have the prehistoric thriller making $8 million through its sophomore weekend (a 62% drop), pushing its North American total to about $37 million.

schema.headline: Box Office: ‘Insidious: Out of the Further’ Takes First Place on Friday With $10.6 Million, But ‘Spider-Man: Brand New Day’ Will Win the Weekend

title: ‘Everything That’s Wrong With You’ Review: A  Luminous Two-Hander from Slovenia About Online Pals Navigating the Waters of IRL Friendship
description: Anyone with a scrolling habit will know that social media can be a soothing place for the downbeat and lonely. Yet the intimacy you can strike up wi
body:
Anyone with a scrolling habit will know that social media can be a soothing place for the downbeat and lonely. Yet the intimacy you can strike up with strangers rubs up against the uncomfortable fact that our online personae are always manipulated to an extent. Writer-director Urša Menart’s luminous Sarajevo competition title “Everything That’s Wrong With You” doesn’t dismiss the potential power of our virtual bonds so much as it recognizes that they operate by a strange and slippery set of rules. Mernart’s sophomore feature, following the 2018 dramedy “My Last Year as a Loser,” continues her exploration of the zillennial blues, offering a Slovenian riff on female friendship indies like “Frances Ha,” grounded by the sweet-and-sour chemistry of its leading ladies. 
	

	In the wake of her mother’s death by cancer, Maruša (Anuša Kodelja), a Daria-esque brunette with a piercing deadpan, finds solace in the bubbly-bleak content produced by wannabe influencer Alja (Klara Kuk), a cute-core blonde who wryly broadcasts her mental health struggles to her followers. When Maruša slides into Alja’s DMs, the two begin texting nonstop as Maruša empties out her mom’s apartment in Ljubljana, settles her debts with former friends, and tenuously reconnects with her cranky father and his family in the Lithuanian countryside. But instead of heading back to Berlin, where she lived before her mother’s illness, she spontaneously takes a bus — the longhaired dachshund she inherited from her mother in tow — to a destination that Menart reveals upon her arrival: the German beach town where Alja lives by herself.
	

	Against the backdrop of this handsomely melancholic coastal setting, whose empty offseason cinematographer Roy Van Egmond captures in desaturated pearl-blue tones, “Everything That’s Wrong You” tracks the transition of the women’s friendship from the screen realm to the more precarious IRL one. At first disaster seems likely when wild-child Maruša shows up to Alja’s neatly maintained apartment unannounced, startlingly blasé about imposing her company through the New Year festivities. 

	Their relationship, against the odds, blooms over bundled-up beach walks and cozy nights-in where the two quip about yearning for lobotomies and wanting to put their “brain[s] in bleach.” The mousier Alja is enlivened by Maruša’s no-fucks-given approach to life, finding in her new (and perhaps first ever) bestie the kind of relationship she thought only happened in movies; Maruša, who mutters about the liars and cheats she used to know in Berlin, is game to play the ride-or-die, dragging Alja out to boozy parties, sharing earbuds, and breaking into the luxe abode of the married man who broke her heart. Kuk and especially Kodelka shine with naturalistic charm in this delicate two-hander, their easy chemistry making credible the rapport between Maruša’s grungy cynic and Alja’s snuggie-wearing neurotic. 

	This black-pink yin-and-yang frays as time together reveals the depths of each character’s dysfunctions, and their camaraderie veers into codependence. Alja, who works at an elder care facility, is a bit too eager to host the freeloading Maruša. Her health problems and submissive, self-effacing nature have left her friendless beyond the guys she meets through dating apps, putting Maruša in a situation where she’s playing caretaker to a new loved one while still grieving the last person she tended. And as Maruša pushes back her departure again and again, Alja’s behavior becomes more erratic — dark and deeply sad revelations that Menart tempers with a delicately irreverent sense of humor. 

	The camera loves Maruša’s pink-puffer-clad dachshund a bit too much, so the duo’s climactic fallout unfolds just as expected, and with a resolution that borders on situational comedy. Menart’s script does a fine job of building out these jagged women with a sharp eye for the growing pains of flesh-and-bones relationships born from the seed of virtual connection. It’s the winsome performers that give this modest film an extra punch to perhaps launch it beyond its regional context.

schema.headline: ‘Everything That’s Wrong With You’ Review: A  Luminous Two-Hander from Slovenia About Online Pals Navigating the Waters of IRL Friendship

title: Actor Michael Wright, Star of ‘The Five Heartbeats’ and ‘V,’ Dies at 70
description: Michael Wright, an actor known for his roles in “The Five Heartbeats,” “Streamers,” “The Principal” and “V,” has died, according to a statement from
body:
Michael Wright, an actor known for his roles in “The Five Heartbeats,” “Streamers,” “The Principal” and “V,” has died, according to a statement from his family. He was 70.

	His wife, Susan Wright, announced his death in a post shared Friday evening on Instagram. “It is with profound sadness and an unimaginable heaviness in my heart that I share the passing of my beloved husband, Michael Wright,” her statement read.


	Wright’s family said he died in Los Angeles on Wednesday, Aug. 19, after suffering heart failure coupled with complications of degenerative neurological disease Marchiafava-Bignami, according to a statement provided to TMZ.
	

	Wright was born on April 30, 1956, in New York City. He appeared in more than 50 movies and TV shows, including the films “The Five Heartbeats,” Robert Altman’s Vietnam drama “Streamers,” “Sugar Hill” and “The Wanderers.” His TV credits include the 1980s sci-fi series “V” and HBO’s “Oz.” In the Robert Townsend-directed 1991 musical film “The Five Heartbeats,” about a fictional Motown group, Wright played the band’s charismatic lead vocalist, Eddie King Jr., whose alcohol and drug addiction forces him to leave the Heartbeats.

	“Michael was a husband, a father (Manon Wright, Byron Barr, Brittney Briggs, Brianna Barr, Sir Barr, a grandfather (Yoko), loved one, a friend, and an extraordinary artist whose work touched generations,” Susan’s statement said. “Many knew and loved him through ‘The Five Heartbeats,’ ‘The Wanderers,’ ‘V,’ ‘The Principal,’ ‘Streamers,’ and the many other characters he brought to life throughout his remarkable career. His talent, presence, and contributions to film and television will live on, but to those of us who loved him personally, he was so much more than the roles the world knew him for.”
	

	Her statement continued, “Our family is grieving an enormous and deeply personal loss. We understand how much Michael meant to so many people, and we are grateful for the love, prayers, memories, and condolences already being shared. … In the coming days, when we are ready, we will share additional information regarding Michael’s life, legacy, and how we intend to honor and celebrate him.”

	Susan concluded, “Michael, your work will live forever, but your love will live even longer in the hearts of those who knew you best. Rest peacefully, my love. You will be missed beyond words.”

	In a 2021 interview with Sheen Magazine, Wright said, “The greatest sin an actor can commit is to fail to be interesting. I always try to make my characters interesting. I want you to be riveted and wonder what’s going on behind my eyes.” Wright also said there wasn’t anything in his life he would do over: “I’ve done everything I have wanted to do. I’ve been everywhere, I speak five different languages. I have seen the world; I love my experiences.”

schema.headline: Actor Michael Wright, Star of ‘The Five Heartbeats’ and ‘V,’ Dies at 70

title: Emily Watson Says ‘Dune: Prophecy’ Season 2 Will Have ‘Lots of New Elements,’ Led Her on ‘A Quest in a Way Actors Always Get to Do and Actresses Don’t’
description: Starring in HBO Max’s “Dune: Prophecy” has been a major “departure” for Emily Watson, whose lauded career was built upon major independent and artho
body:
Starring in HBO Max’s “Dune: Prophecy” has been a major “departure” for Emily Watson, whose lauded career was built upon major independent and arthouse successes such as Lars von Trier’s “Breaking the Waves” and Robert Altman’s “Gosford Park.” As she embarks on a second season of the hit show, the actress feels more settled in the sprawling sci-fi world, she noted at the Variety Lounge, presented by the Sarajevo Film Festival and BH Telecom.
	

	“It was a true departure for me to be in a spaceship,” she said. “You know, it’s actually really good fun.” Speaking about reprising her role as Valya Harkonnen in the upcoming second season of the series, which has been shot but still has no release date, Watson said she experienced a “sense of being on a quest in a way that actors always get to do and actresses don’t. And that was just fun.” 

	Asked if she could share anything about the highly secretive series, the actress offered a brief tease: “There are a lot of new elements, really interesting and intriguing things […] I think my head will blow off if I mention any of them,” she quipped. 

	What about another major upcoming entry in the “Dune” world with Denis Villeneuve’s “Dune: Part Three”? “I mean, I can’t wait to see that movie,” she promptly responded. “I’m a huge fan of him, obviously, and it’s stuffed full of incredible actors that I love.”

	Watson recalled first stepping into the massive “Dune” world: “It’s HBO Max, it’s huge. A lot of money. It’s a sense of it being much more than a corporate world. But it was a big ensemble of young women, some young men, who were all relatively new to the business.” The veteran has often spoken about her affinity for mentoring young performers, and she reiterated this desire when embarking on “Prophecy.”
	

	The actress recalled “how hard” it is to be away from family for long periods of shooting. “Putting it all together is a challenge,” she said, adding that, “especially in the world of independent film,” it is all about “relationships.” 

	“I always give people advice to nurture a relationship with somebody less experienced,” she noted. “Interconnectedness is how we all survive. Surviving in the world of independent film is hard. There are so many things that fall by the wayside, get destroyed and steamrolled. If we are all together, we are stronger, and I think building relationships with more inexperienced people is really important.” 

	Watson first came to Sarajevo in 2005, as a curator of the Katrin Cartlidge Foundation. Her screen partner on “Breaking the Waves” died aged 41 in 2002, with Sarajevo setting up a filmmaking bursary in her name shortly after. Speaking about being back in Bosnia so many years later, now as the president of the jury and the recipient of a Heart of Sarajevo Award, Watson said it’s been “quite overwhelming.” 

	The actress revisited Von Trier’s film at this year’s festival, which she called a “very emotional” experience, mostly because of her deep connection to Cartlidge. “Also just being here, meeting all these incredible filmmakers, seeing these amazing films… This festival feels like the pure form of what a festival should be. It embodies the idea that culture is resistance.”

	As for what is next, on top of the new season of “Dune: Prophecy,” Watson also recently shot Mira Nair’s historical drama “AMRI.” The film depicts the life of the Hungarian-Indian painter Amrita Sher-Gil, with Watson playing the artist’s mother. “I left Harkonnen and went straight to that,” recalled the actress. 

	“I’m playing a Hungarian woman, so we were shooting in Budapest, then we went to India, and I was suddenly surrounded by Indian actors and crew with Mira, and it was the most amazing adventure,” she said. “It’s a really interesting story. I can’t wait to see how that comes out. They’re in editing now, so we’ll see, but [Nair] is an extraordinary filmmaker and an amazing person to be around. She is one of those people who kind of gathers an energy and a force. It was amazing.”

schema.headline: Emily Watson Says ‘Dune: Prophecy’ Season 2 Will Have ‘Lots of New Elements,’ Led Her on ‘A Quest in a Way Actors Always Get to Do and Actresses Don’t’

title: Andrew Garfield on His Secret Instagram, Thoughts of Leaving Hollywood and Playing Roy in the ‘Stranger Than Fiction’ Siegfried & Roy Television Series
description:
Andrew Garfield admits he has a secret Instagram account.

	“I’m as addicted as anybody. My screen time notifications are horrific to me. It’s like,
body:
Andrew Garfield admits he has a secret Instagram account.

	“I’m as addicted as anybody. My screen time notifications are horrific to me. It’s like, I’ve given all of those hours to nothing,” he says. “It’s genuinely enraging because we don’t have as much control over these impulses as we should, and it’s been by design. It’s pretty dark when you look at it.”

	His Instagram rabbit holes include “weird ceramics” and “lots of Japanese kind of craftspeople.” 
	

	Social media and technology are at the heart of Garfield’s new film, “The Magic Faraway Tree,” an adaptation of the Enid Blyton book series that is in theaters now. He and Claire Foy play Tim and Polly, a London couple who pack up their lives and their tech-dependent kids and move to a farm in the country. Their youngest child, Fran (Billie Gadsdon), doesn’t speak until she discovers a magical tree inhabited by elf-like creatures.


	I spoke to Garfield talks about his busy year ahead — he also stars in the upcoming action period drama “The Uprising,” plays Sam Altman in Luca Guadagnino’s “Artificial” and portrays Roy in the Siegfried & Roy TV series “Wild Things” — and what he dreams of doing when he’s not working.
	
		In “Faraway Tree,” your characters move to the country because it was a dream they wrote in their “dream binder” when they got married 15 years ago. What was in your dream binder 15 years ago?	

	I was 27. What was I doing then?
	
		Oh, you know.	

	I was doing “Spider-Man.” That was a dream from 40 years ago, so I was checking off one of my big dreams. I was also checking off just being an actor. I still have dreams, but they’re slightly more earthbound than my previous ones. They’re maybe a bit more philosophical and existential than achievement based. Now I think it’s more I want a certain quality of life. I want a certain quality of relationships with my family and friends. I want a certain quality of relationship with myself.
	
	
		Have you ever thought about leaving it all behind?	

	All the time. I’ve worked a lot this year. I’ve done like 11 months, 12 months, straight back-to-back projects. I want people to see those projects, so I’m gonna have to tell people about them. I get that. But if I had my druthers, people would just see them, and I could go whittle wood in the Somerset countryside and think about what the birds might be doing.
	
		Tim and Polly are constantly trying to get the kids off their phones and tablets. Do you ever go on a phone detox?	

	I think we’ve all had the impulse to smash our phones or throw it into the forest or throw it into the sea because we know it’s taking our lives from us in some way. I’m not better than anybody else. I’ve been told, and I find it to be true, that if you leave your phone in another room, that does a lot of the heavy lifting. As soon as it’s in the room, you’re kind of fucked.
	
		I sometimes put it in the trunk of my car so I don’t look at it while I’m driving. But then I’ll pull over, take it out of the trunk and keep driving.	

	Wow! You’ve got a problem, a big problem.
	
		I like to tell myself it’s all for work.	

	We’ll justify addiction in whatever way we can.
	
		Were phones banned on set?	

	They weren’t, but you know they didn’t really need to be. Our intention with the film wasn’t to damn technology. We didn’t want to say that all technology is evil and bad. We wanted to just have a healthier relationship with it. That was the ethos on set as well. We don’t need to ban stuff, but we just don’t want to be completely taken over by these things.
	
		Judi Dench voices a smart fridge in the movie. Was this your first time working with her?	

	[Laughs] It was our first time. I didn’t even know I was working with her. It was retrospective. At the time of filming, it was just an imagined voice. And now, God, if I had known it was Judi, I would have played it differently. What an amazing woman! What a legend.
	
		How did “Wild Things” come about?	

	I signed up about a year and a half before we started shooting, and then Jude came on. It was like, “Oh my God, Jude Law as Siegfried? Fuck, yes! I need to be front row for that.” I love him like my brother now.
	
		What got you so interested in the project?	

	Their lives are stranger than fiction. It’s been a really challenging shoot and very, very rewarding. There’s not only this pizzazz and style and aesthetic and camp, but there’s also a big heart and soul underneath it. There’s a woundedness, a longing, and there’s love, and there’s danger. The stakes couldn’t be higher. You’re going to be giddy and giggling in your seat.

title: Austrian Director Sandra Wollner’s ‘Everytime’ Wins Best Film at Sarajevo Film Festival
description: Sandra Wollner’s “Everytime” continued its winning streak at the Sarajevo Film Festival, where the Cannes Un Certain Regard winner took home the Hea
body:
Sandra Wollner’s “Everytime” continued its winning streak at the Sarajevo Film Festival, where the Cannes Un Certain Regard winner took home the Heart of Sarajevo for best narrative feature film.

	The Austrian director’s third feature was the unanimous choice of a jury headed by two-time Academy Award nominee Emily Watson, which said in its citation: “Moments of cinematic grace float through this mesmerically elastic and transcendental grief-soaked ghost story.”
	

	“Everytime” follows a mother, young daughter and teenage boy who, united by tragedy, embark on a trip to the Canary Islands for a family holiday that never happened. Under the glow of the coastal sun, past and present begin to quietly overlap. 


	Following its premiere at the Cannes Film Festival, Variety’s chief film critic Guy Lodge praised Wollner’s “poised, haunting” drama, noting that it “confirms the Austrian director’s formidable formal control and imagination, and should be her most widely distributed work to date.”

	The Heart of Sarajevo for best director went to Georgian filmmaker Ana Urushadze for “Supporting Role,” another festival darling that scooped two prizes in Rotterdam earlier this year. In another unanimous choice, the jury members said they were “enchanted by [Urushadze’s] irreverent blending of the banal and the oneiric, and her refreshing curiosity for meaning in life and cinema.” 

	Variety’s Beatrice Loayza was likewise swept up by the “mesmerizing effect” of the director’s moody, meandering drama, which follows “a lumbering movie star on a surreal and wryly melancholic soul-search” on the streets of Tbilisi.
	

	The award for best actress went to Eva Kostić for her lead role in “17,” the debut feature from North Macedonian director Kosara Mitić, about a teenager on a class trip wrestling with the aftermath of a sexual assault. The jury heralded her performance as “raw, visceral and deeply instinctive” and the “fearless emergence of a young talent,” adding “She brings an extraordinary emotional truth to the role, announcing the arrival of an actress with a rare and powerful voice.”

	Best actor honors went to Adrian Văncică for “You Don’t Belong Here,” Romanian filmmaker Florin Şerban’s Locarno Golden Leopard winner about a respected doctor whose world is shaken when he discovers his son is a suspect in the murder of a Roma man. The jury praised Văncică “for a performance marked by tenacity and understated rigor, in which the actor consistently serves a story directed in long and wide shots.”

	The Heart of Sarajevo for best documentary feature went to directing duo by Biljana Tutorov and Petar Glomazić for “To Hold a Mountain,” a story of sisterhood and solitude in the Montenegrin highlands. The film, which won the World Cinema Grand Jury Prize at Sundance and the Grand Prix at Poland’s Millennium Docs Against Gravity, was hailed as “an unforgettable journey” by the documentary jury, which said in its citation: “With astonishingly epic cinematography this touching portrait of two extraordinary women and a disappearing way of life enchanted us.”

	Here’s the complete list of awards for the 32nd Sarajevo Film Festival:

	NARRATIVE FEATURE FILM

	Best Narrative Feature Film: “Everytime,” Sandra Wollner 

	Best Director: Ana Urushadze, “Supporting Role”

	Best Actress: Eva Kostić, “17” 

	Best Actor: Adrian Văncică, “You Don’t Belong Here”

	DOCUMENTARY FILM

	Best Documentary Feature Film: “To Hold a Mountain,” Biljana Tutorov, Petar Glomazić 

	Best Short Documentary Film: “Holy Defiance,” Karla Jelić 

	Special Jury Award: “The Ferry Flows,” Zhora Papoian 

	NARRATIVE SHORT FILM

	Best Narrative Short Film: “Nobody Said Anything,” Tamara Todorović 
	

	Special Mention: “Porkatal,” Sis Gürdal 

	STUDENT SHORT FILM 

	Best Student Short Film: “Unwellness,” Réka Pinczés 

	SPECIAL AWARDS

	Special Award for Promoting Gender Equality: “17,” Kosara Mitić 

	Special Mention: “Don’t Ask Me if I Killed,” Helena Maksyom 

	Special Youth Perspectives Award: “Skateboarding is Not for Girls,” Dina Duma

	Katrin Cartlidge Foundation Award: Lana Daher

title: Olivia Rodrigo Releases ‘Handmaid’s Tale’-Inspired Song, ‘Serena Joy,’ in a Tiny Run of CDs, With Digital Drop to Follow
description: It was already clear Olivia Rodrigo is in full feminist mode these days, with her all-female music festival, Daisy Chain Fields, set to take place i
body:
It was already clear Olivia Rodrigo is in full feminist mode these days, with her all-female music festival, Daisy Chain Fields, set to take place in California’s Orange County next Saturday. But it’s perhaps even clearer now that Rodrigo is releasing a non-album track, “Serena Joy,” named after a prominent character in “The Handmaid’s Tale” who comes to regret her complicity with a repressive patriarchy. 

	“Serena Joy” was released Friday as a very limited-edition CD single, with only 500 units pressed, all of them available exclusively at a single record store, Analog Music Shop in Tustin, Calif. (The store reported Friday night that all 500 copies had sold through.)
	

	Of course, the song won’t be heard exclusively in Orange County CD players for long. Analog Music Shop — which so far seems to be the only source of official information about the track — reported that Rodrigo’s plan is to send it out wide to the world on Monday.


	The existence of a song titled “Serena Joy” had already been confirmed by Rodrigo in June, after fans spotted the title in a studio photograph listing 18 songs that were under consideration for her “You Look Pretty Sad for a Girl So in Love” album.

	Asked about it in a video interview with Etalk two months ago, Rodrigo smiled and said, “I actually really love [“Serena Joy”]. It didn’t fit on the album. The record was very much a chronicle of a relationship — beginning, middle and end. But I hope that it’ll be a part of something else down the line.”

	On Friday morning, Analog Music Shop posted about the song and its exclusive availability. “When we heard that Olivia Rodrigo was bringing an all-women music festival to Orange County, we were honestly just excited to see something this special happening right here in our hometown” (using “hometown” loosely, but close enough, since Tustin is adjacent to Irvine, where Daisy Chain Fields is taking place). “As one of the closest record stores in the area, we wanted to find a way to support Daisy Chain Fields.”
	

	The message continued, “We knew Olivia had a track record of supporting record stores, but we were still taken aback when we heard the news: Olivia is releasing a new song ahead of Daisy Chain Fields called ‘Serena Joy,’ and she wants the physical CD copies to be exclusively sold at Analog Record Shop. And the best part… She’s giving it to us 3 DAYS before anyone else can hear it. Three days early. More than anything, we’re grateful for what this represents: An artist building a stage for women in music and raising funds for women and girls. An artist willing to support a local independent record store. And a hometown getting to be part of something really special. That means a lot to us.”

	No one had to wait to hear or at least see the lyrics, at least, since they were printed right on the front of the CD, in images disseminated by the shop. Inevitably, the music itself was leaked, although takedown orders were issued.

	The lyrics do not mention the Serena Joy character or any other overt “Handmaid’s Tale” references, but with that as the title, the meaning of verses that might otherwise seem vague can be seen in fairly clear focus.

	“Yeah, it’s all for the cause / For the good of us all / And if you close your eyes / Then it can’t be your fault,” Rodrigo sings at the outset, in cautionary-tale lyrics. “Here’s a tower we built / Painted gold on the walls,” she adds in the lines that follow, possibly alluding to the popularity of literal gold-leaf in certain circles in the current age.

	The key recurring lyrics: “If they do it to them / They’ll do it to you / If they do it to them / They’re gonna do it to you.” Those are the clearest referrals to the “Handmaid’s Tale” character, who is one of the few women who seems to have a position of power in the patriarchy that has taken over a future America, yet who comes to find that she will be just as oppressed and endangered as any woman under the system she helped build.

	As Margaret Atwood writes of Serena Joy in the novel that inspired the television series: “She doesn’t make speeches anymore. She has become speechless. She stays in her home, but it doesn’t seem to agree with her. How furious she must be, now that she’s been taken at her word.”

	Many fans reacting online to the new song were down with the thought of Rodrigo stretching her political wings a little in song, even if most were in agreement that it would have been a poor fit with the tight relationship focus of “You Seem Pretty Sad for a Girl So in Love.”
	

	“Forget hot girl summer we’re entering our dystopian propaganda era,” wrote one fan commenting on the song’s Genius lyrics page. Wrote another, along similar lines, “Hot girl summer into fascism fall.”

schema.headline: Olivia Rodrigo Releases ‘Handmaid’s Tale’-Inspired Song, ‘Serena Joy,’ in a Tiny Run of CDs, With Digital Drop to Follow

title: Bill Maher Puts Hunter Biden in the Hot Seat: ‘I’ve Seen You With Your Dick Out’
description: After enduring years of character assassinations by the right, Hunter Biden is in the throes of a chaotic media blitz that’s included Twitter-trolli
body:
After enduring years of character assassinations by the right, Hunter Biden is in the throes of a chaotic media blitz that’s included Twitter-trolling, posting on Substack and appearances on a number of far-right podcasts, from Hitler worshipper Nick Fuentes and Russia stooge Tucker Carlson to conspiracy theorist Candace Owens. Is Joe Biden’s wayward son trying to land a lucrative podcast deal or taking one last stand to clear his name as his father battles cancer?
	

	Whatever the reason, the latest stop on Biden’s no-holds-barred media tour saw the 56-year-old sit down with Bill Maher on his HBO series “Real Time” Friday night. And their conversation got off to a rollicking start.

	“Your obituary, the third word will be ‘laptop.’ I know everything about the laptop — more things than I want to know. I’ve seen you with your dick out. I’ve seen you with a crack pipe in your mouth. My question: Are you running for president?” cracked Maher, opening things.


	“I’m here to announce…,” joked Biden, before adding, “No, I haven’t [thought of it]. Here’s my thing: If I announce for president then someone should check to see if I’ve relapsed.”

	Throughout their chat, Biden appeared nervous but prepared, opening up about his seven years of sobriety and saying he’s been out there speaking because “there are 50 million Americans that are still sick and suffering every day from addiction, and I get to go out there and I get to speak to them.”



	Maher, meanwhile, mostly treated the Biden offspring with kid gloves, even telling him at one point, “I think I would say to you what I said to Charlie Sheen: You did some bad things, but I don’t think you’re a bad guy.” (Charlie Sheen pleaded guilty to assaulting his ex, among other things.)
	

	Biden also acknowledged his “privilege” and argued that the money he made while his father was vice president was “a fraction of a penny” compared to what the Trump kids have made while their father was president.

	“Just to put it in perspective: In the last 500 days of this administration, Don Jr.’s company has taken in $3.4 billion in Department of Defense contracts. He got a $640 million loan pushed through by the Whtie House… and that’s just a fraction of it,” explained Biden. “Forget about what they’ve done with cryptocurrency, which is a bank where they were able to go and launder their money, which is an abomination, and that doesn’t even include what Jared is doing and Ivanka is doing. He gets paid $100 million in fees by the Saudis alone for a $6.5 billion fund that he controls that’s all Gulf State money, and he’s our unelected, unappointed emissary to the Middle East for a war that nobody asked for.”

	When it comes to his father Joe, who is currently suffering from Stage 4 prostate cancer, Biden said he’s apologized to him “every day” for his mistakes and it’s “one of the greatest heartaches of my life,” adding, “I can never make up for that.”

title: ‘Spa Weekend’ Review: Leslie Mann and Isla Fisher in a High-Concept Comedy Without the Comic Highs
description: Movie genres wax and wane over time in a way that can be borderline imperceptible. The Western did its slow fade through the 1960s, but it took a wh
body:
Movie genres wax and wane over time in a way that can be borderline imperceptible. The Western did its slow fade through the 1960s, but it took a while to realize that it was heading into the sunset (and then, of course, it came back). On a less exalted level, I watched “Spa Weekend” and realized that the genre it’s in — the high-concept comedy with the concept in the title, the movie that puts out a vibe of “Look, I’m crass and dumb and obvious! And that’s why you like me!” — may now be entering its twilight zone.
	

	Written and directed by Jon Lucas and Scott Moore, who made the brashly clever and likable “Bad Moms” (but were launched by their script for “The Hangover,” and in a way they’re still writing it), “Spa Weekend” is a comedy about four old friends who go on a deluxe spa getaway. The film has its minor-league version of a star cast (Leslie Mann, Anna Faris, Michelle Buteau, Isla Fisher), with Fisher cast against type as the Melissa McCarthy character — a foul-mouthed British trainwreck in ridiculously loud clothing who becomes the film’s bull in the aroma-therapy shop.


	It’s all very standard, and the idea of putting the satirical screws to the New Age elitism of wellness culture certainly has potential. But watching “Spa Weekend,” you feel how tired and predictable the jokes are (it’s the script that needs a massage). And I’m talking about the “wild” jokes, like when the women take a raucous golf-cart ride through the spa grounds, or when a divorced couple work off their aggression by having a mud fight in a mud bath, or the moment when a session of “goat yoga” devolves — inevitably — into a Who let the goats out? free-for-all. It’s “anarchic” yet weirdly tame and expected. You watch these rote antics and think: Where are Barb and Star when you need them?
	

	The four women are cardboard-cutout archetypes, played in amiable lightweight fashion. There’s Jane (Mann), a high-strung attorney and divorced single mother whose birthday weekend this is, and who is such an overscheduled control freak that she can only put a date with a man on her calendar three months in advance; Coco (Michelle Buteau), also divorced with two kids, who’s presented as a walking fount of anger issues (though if you call her on it, she’ll get angry at you for reducing her to the “angry Black woman”); Sophie (Anna Faris), a blonde mouse who’s been the personal assistant to a tyrannical boss for 10 years; and Fisher’s bawdy, antic, disheveled Mel, who the other three can’t stand, but as the movie explains — it becomes a central theme — every female friend group needs one person the others secretly hate.

	I had mild hopes for “Spa Weekend” when it introduced the Solaris Eden Beach spa, a luxe white-on-white beachfront hotel that turns pampering into a form of exhibitionism. When Jane and her friends arrive at the front desk, they’re offered a choice of Champagne or hibiscus water, and the spa’s general manager is a guru named Shanti (Erika Keynatz) who glows with well-tended superiority. Then, of course, there’s Kai (Adam Demos), the hot Aussie yoga instructor who makes instant eye contact with Jane (“C’mon, Magic Mike,” says Mel, “let’s see your big ding-dong!”). About 45 minutes in, Jane and Kai run into each at the otherwise empty hotel bar, and Jane explains that she can see right through the posh pretense of the spa treatments — the spaced-out music and yoga that’s just “stretching,” the Goopy optics of it all. But it’s as if the movie had already seen through its own joke.   

	By all rights, Isla Fisher’s Mel should be the one making us laugh. I’ve always been a fan of this actor, and she gives a pinpoint performance as a dissolute narcissist who’s like a more unhinged Bridget Jones. But Fisher, in a weird way, gives too grounded a performance. She doesn’t have that spark plug of trashy insanity in her DNA. (We don’t feel her unconscious need to destroy.) Or maybe the lines just aren’t crazy enough. Frankly, I had the same problem with “The Hangover,” a movie I always thought was more prechewed than it pretended to be. And you wish “Spa Weekend” found a way to give Leslie Mann, the film’s straight-arrow center of gravity, a bit more of a spin.     
	

	“Spa Weekend” is being distributed by Black Bear Pictures — a good company, only this sort of thing used to be the province of major studios, and now it’s being relegated to the indie and streaming market. (See this month’s “Super Troopers 3.”) Nothing wrong with that, of course. But it’s a sign that overly processed bad-behavior comedies like “Spa Weekend” are a form that’s running out of gas. What happens at the spa stays at the spa. But it might as well not, since we’ve seen it before.

            "The Challenge" star Tyler Duckworth was tragically found "up against the door" of his bathroom when he died.
      
    
            A case report from the Grand Forks Police Department -- obtained by Page Six -- said that's how the 44-year-old's body was found in his North Dakota apartment.
      
    
            The person reporting also said they had a tough time reaching the former MTV competitor, according to the outlet.
      

            The report described how the downstairs neighbor -- who had complained of water coming through the ceiling from Tyler's overflowing bathtub -- "tried to get the water shut off" and was "not able to confirm" whether Tyler was alive.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            As we previously reported, Grand Forks PD told TMZ ... officers found no outward signs of trauma -- including no gunshot or stab wounds -- and preliminary findings show no indication Tyler's death was a homicide.

title: NYC Grandma Who Went Missing In Las Vegas Tumbled Down Embankment, Police Say
description:
Missing NYC Grandma
                          Tumbled Down Embankment by Vegas Airport
body:
Missing NYC Grandma
                          Tumbled Down Embankment by Vegas Airport
                          Many Questions Remain
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              August 21, 2026
                            5:21 PM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            The case of a New York City grandma who's been missing for two weeks in Las Vegas took a sad turn Thursday ... and TMZ is learning more about what happened to the 63-year-old.
      
    
            Alisa Goods was visiting a friend in Sin City, and she left their home on August 8 to go shopping at CVS and vanished. Days after she disappeared, someone began messaging from her phone, asking her family for bitcoin. She was found dead Thursday near Harry Reid International Airport.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Las Vegas Metro PD tells TMZ ... surveillance from the airport shows a woman, believed to be Goods, falling down an embankment -- getting back up and then collapsing on August 8.
      

            As we previously reported ... it was the area surveillance that led authorities to her body ... but why she was there wandering around -- and who was using her phone afterward -- are total mysteries.
      
    
                    
                          
                                  
      
        
    
            Police are playing this one close to the vest -- and won't comment on the cause or manner of death -- but her family ... along with everyone else following the case that's made national headlines, want answers.
